specAnchors.text: know that specific heat capacity is the energy required to change the temperature of an object by one degree Celsius per kilogram of mass (J/kg °C)
use the equation: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × change in temperature Δ Q = m × c × ΔT

primer.text: Different substances are differently stubborn about warming: water soaks up four thousand joules per kilogram per degree, metals far less. This note defines specific heat capacity, contrasts the high-capacity and low-capacity worlds, and drills the ΔQ = mcΔT calculation to a two-significant-figure finish.

modules.title: Defining specific heat capacity
modules.opening: Specific heat capacity is the price, in joules, of lifting one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius. High-capacity substances are slow to warm and slow to cool; low-capacity substances sprint through both.
keyPoints: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to warm 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.
Its unit is joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, written J/kg °C.
Water has a high specific heat capacity, so it warms up and cools down slowly.
Substances with a low specific heat capacity heat up and cool down quickly for the same energy.
The temperature change for a given energy input depends on the mass and the material heated.

low.restatement: Think of specific heat capacity as a per-kilogram, per-degree price tag. Water's tag is about 4200 J/kg °C, so a kettle needs thousands of joules for every single degree on every single kilogram.
low.analogy: Filling buckets of different widths: the same jug of energy raises the narrow bucket (low capacity) far faster than the wide one (high capacity).
low.examPointer: Always attach all three units — J/kg °C — because dropping the 'per kilogram' or the 'per degree' makes the definition wrong on the mark scheme.

medium.restatement: The definition is energetic, not thermal-intuitive: it is the energy per unit mass per unit temperature rise stored by the substance's particles. A high capacity means much of the supplied energy goes into the substance's internal store per degree, so temperature responds sluggishly in both heating and cooling directions.
medium.analogy: A wide harbour versus a narrow pool fed by the same stream: the harbour's level (temperature) creeps up while the pool leaps, even though the inflow (power) is identical.
medium.examPointer: Comparison questions want the consequence chain: higher capacity means slower warming AND slower cooling — quote both directions or the mark is half-earned.

modules.title: Calculating with ΔQ = mcΔT
modules.opening: One triangle equation runs the whole topic: change in thermal energy equals mass times specific heat capacity times temperature change. Rearranged, it also yields capacity from experiment data — the bridge to the core practical that follows this note.
keyPoints: The equation is ΔQ = m × c × ΔT for a temperature change with no change of state.
ΔQ is the change in thermal energy in joules, m the mass in kilograms, c the specific heat capacity, ΔT the temperature change in °C.
Rearranged forms give c = ΔQ ÷ (mΔT) and ΔT = ΔQ ÷ (mc).
Final answers should be quoted to an appropriate number of significant figures.
The equation applies only while the substance stays in one state — latent heat governs melting and boiling instead.

low.restatement: Multiply the mass by the capacity by the temperature change and you have the energy bill. Know any three of the four quantities and the fourth falls out by rearranging.
low.analogy: A restaurant bill: heads (mass) times set-menu price (capacity) times rounds (degrees) equals the total (energy).
low.examPointer: Write the equation first, substitute second, and quote units last — the three-line layout collects all the method marks.

medium.restatement: ΔQ = mcΔT quantifies the kinetic-energy store change of the particles: heavier samples and high-capacity substances demand proportionally more energy per degree. The rearrangement c = ΔQ/(mΔT) is exactly how the immersion-heater practical measures capacity, turning two meter readings and a thermometer into a material property.
medium.analogy: A toll road: total fare (ΔQ) scales with the number of vehicles (m), the per-vehicle rate (c), and the number of zones crossed (ΔT) — know three, recover the fourth.
medium.examPointer: Check the state before calculating: across a melting or boiling plateau ΔT is zero and the equation would wrongly return zero energy — that regime belongs to latent heat.

glossary.definition: The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C, in J/kg °C.
The internal energy of a substance associated with its particle motion and temperature.
The digits of an answer that carry meaningful precision given the inputs.

workedExample.prompt: Water of mass 0.48 kg is increased in temperature by 0.7 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. Calculate the amount of thermal energy transferred to the water.
steps: List the known quantities: mass m = 0.48 kg, temperature change ΔT = 0.7 °C, specific heat capacity c = 4200 J/kg °C.
Write the relevant equation: ΔQ = m × c × ΔT.
Round the answer to 2 significant figures: ΔQ = 1400 J.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The thermal energy transferred to the water is 1400 J (2 s.f.).
